Gold is not an investment, it is disinvestment from everything. People are taking economic sanyas when they buy Gold.

Nirmala Sitaraman the Indian finance minister is taxing citizens heavily,taxing Gold and buying gold! Why? 

Buying Gold is ultimate disinvestment. Tax to disinvest? Government disinvesting in itself.

Talk of currency stabilization is nonsense. Why not private banks and temples issue gold backed private money. Competition is always better than monopoly.

Before  first world war German government cornered , seized all the gold it could lay it's hands on.

Gold prices shoots up in war. German government, TAX EATERS, made huge profit even when Germany lost the war. Millions were sacrificed to tax eaters.

Governments should not hold gold – and only private agencies should. Governments holding gold is hedging against tax payers so that it has incentive to create Chaos and profit from it (Public choice theory) ruining the people.

HOW GOVERNMENTS EAT TOMORROW'S HARVEST 

India's declining birth rate should concern anyone interested in long-term prosperity. A child is not merely a consumer but an investment in the future. Under normal market conditions, productive businesses should outperform gold because they create new wealth, whereas gold merely preserves existing wealth. When gold consistently outperforms productive enterprise, the market is signalling that capital is fleeing from production toward protection against political risk. Investors no longer trust the monetary and fiscal regime.

Parents devote decades of time, money, and effort to raising children because they expect the next generation to enjoy a better life than they did. The modern tax state steadily undermines this expectation. If children's future earnings are increasingly consumed through taxation, public debt, and inflation, the incentive to invest in the next generation inevitably weakens. A society that rewards hoarding gold while making children more expensive through taxes and inflation is consuming the seed capital of civilization itself.

1. THE CONCEPT OF SEED MONEY

The greatest economic error of the modern state is that it consumes seed money. A farmer who eats his seed before planting guarantees a poor harvest. Likewise, a government that taxes capital before it is invested guarantees lower capital accumulation, lower productivity, lower wages, and lower future living standards.

Taxation without consent is institutionalized theft. Yet some taxes are even more destructive than others because they seize capital before it has the opportunity to multiply. Income tax, capital gains tax, inheritance tax, wealth taxes, and the Securities Transaction Tax are all taxes on seed money. They consume the seed instead of waiting for the harvest.

Even if one grants, purely for argument's sake, that some taxation is unavoidable, economic logic points in only one direction: tax ONLY  final consumption, never production, saving, investment, or capital formation. Taxes imposed upstream of consumption distort entrepreneurial calculation by falsifying the price signals upon which markets depend. They reduce investment long before they reduce consumption.

India goes even further. It taxes stock market transactions through the Securities Transaction Tax (STT), meaning that even unsuccessful investments are taxed. Imagine taxing a failed business merely because it attempted to produce wealth. That is not economics; it resembles a protection racket.

The same confusion appears in the taxation of capital gains. Central banks expand the money supply, pushing up nominal asset prices. Governments then tax these purely monetary gains as though they represented genuine increases in wealth. Inflation first reduces the purchasing power of money, and the tax system then confiscates the illusionary "gain" created by that very inflation. Citizens lose twice.

Taxing gold or Bitcoin is still worse because these assets often represent the preservation of capital against monetary depreciation. Taxing them is equivalent to taxing people for attempting to protect their savings from inflation. It is taxation at the furthest upstream point of the production process.

The irony is complete when politicians and bureaucrats, after consuming domestic capital through taxation, inflation, and regulation, travel abroad at taxpayers' expense seeking foreign investment. The monopoly state destroys domestic seed money and then asks foreigners to provide new seed. It is circular logic repeated every election cycle.

2. PROTECTIONISM: SELF-IMPOSED SANCTIONS

Protectionism is simply self-imposed sanctions. Tariffs do not primarily punish foreign producers; they punish domestic consumers and domestic industries that depend upon imported machinery, technology, and raw materials. They distort the structure of production by directing investment according to political privilege rather than consumer demand.

As Ludwig von Mises emphasized, production exists for consumption. Protectionism reverses this principle by forcing consumers to subsidize politically protected producers. The beneficiaries are concentrated and politically organized; the consumers who bear the costs are numerous and unorganized. Public Choice economics explains why such policies survive despite making society poorer.

Tariffs also institutionalize rent-seeking. Instead of competing through innovation and efficiency, firms compete for political favours. Bureaucracies expand, corruption becomes profitable, and smuggling naturally follows. Every prohibition creates its own black market.

Economic nationalism often spills into political nationalism. Bastiat warned, "When goods do not cross borders, armies will." Free trade encourages peaceful cooperation because it rewards mutual gain. Protectionism encourages political conflict because it rewards privilege.

As Matt Ridley observed, there is not a single example of a country opening itself to trade and becoming poorer. Trade creates wealth; tariffs merely redistribute it.

3. ECONOMICS AND MORALITY

Economics explains consequences; it does not determine morality. Even a theoretically efficient tax cannot answer the ethical question of whether coercive confiscation is justified. Nor can economic statistics measure the long-term effects of dependence upon the state, the erosion of personal responsibility, or the destruction of individual initiative.

History likewise demonstrates the danger of abandoning equality before the law. Once governments accept the principle that different groups may legitimately be treated differently, confiscation often becomes the first step toward more serious forms of persecution –including genocide.

4. MONEY, ENTREPRENEURSHIP, AND REAL WEALTH

Central Bank Digital Currency represents the logical extension of monetary centralization. Cash permits permissionless exchange. A centrally controlled digital currency has the potential to transform money into an instrument of surveillance and administrative control.

The Observer Research Foundation's 2022 report "Jailed for Doing Business" identified more than 26,000 imprisonment provisions affecting entrepreneurs under Union and State laws. Enterprise increasingly operates under political permission rather than commercial freedom.

GDP also exaggerates prosperity by counting government expenditure as though it were equivalent to productive output. Murray Rothbard's concept of Private Product Remaining (PPR) better reflects the wealth that actually remains with producers after state consumption. As Gurucharan Das remarked, "India grows when government sleeps." The Austrian economist would add: societies prosper when entrepreneurs—not politicians—allocate capital.

CONCLUSION

The lesson is simple. Prosperity depends upon preserving seed money.

Tax capital before it is invested, and future wealth never comes into existence.

Inflate the currency, tax nominal gains, and call the result "economic management."

Protect inefficient producers through tariffs, and consumers become poorer while political privilege expands.

Governments cannot consume tomorrow's harvest without first eating today's seed.

The road to prosperity is therefore equally simple: protect private property, tax consumption—if taxation must exist at all—rather than capital, preserve sound money, abolish protectionism, and allow entrepreneurs rather than politicians to determine the allocation of resources.

Eat the seed, and the harvest disappears.
Plant the seed, and civilization prospers.
